title: *CS510 GDB Solution*
text:
*CS510 GDB Solution*

Selected Technique: JAD Workshops

If I were the Lead Requirements Engineer, I would select JAD Workshops as the primary technique for eliciting requirements. The main reason is that the project involves a major commercial bank where confidential customer information and strict security policies make on-site observation difficult.

JAD workshops bring fraud analysts, developers, and management together to discuss operational workflows, business rules, and system requirements. This encourages stakeholder participation, allows immediate clarification of misunderstandings, and helps resolve conflicting opinions. It is also more time-efficient and cost-effective because requirements can be discussed and finalized in a few scheduled sessions.

On-site observation, on the other hand, provides more authentic information about actual workplace practices. It helps identify routine activities, implicit knowledge, and time-sensitive decisions that analysts might forget to explain. However, arranging multiple observation sessions can be expensive and time-consuming. Restricted access to banking systems and sensitive information also creates organizational challenges.

To overcome the limitation of JAD workshops, I would recommend conducting short follow-up interviews with selected fraud analysts after the workshops. They can explain their daily activities and provide examples of unusual cases without sharing confidential customer details. The gathered information can then be used to validate and improve the documented requirements.

In my opinion, JAD workshops offer a better balance of stakeholder involvement, cost, time, and organizational security for this project while follow-up discussions can help capture missing practical details.
